opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that nobody really knows, and that's part of what makes the situation somewhat concerning. What we can observe is that if you take these very large circuits, transformers with hundreds of billions of parameters, and you train them on more and more text, their ability to predict the next word keeps getting better. And along with that, you get these apparently emergent capabilities: answering questions, writing code, doing some forms of reasoning.

My suspicion is that a lot of what's happening is that the system is building up an enormous library of patterns, fragments of text, fragments of reasoning, and ways of putting them together. When you have trillions of words of training data, you're covering a huge fraction of the kinds of things human beings say and write. So a lot of the performance comes from the system having seen something sufficiently similar before and being able to adapt it. That's not nothing. It's actually quite impressive. But it's different from building a coherent internal model of the world and reasoning from it in the way we'd expect from a genuinely intelligent system.

One piece of evidence for this is that these systems often fail in ways that a human who actually understood the concepts would never fail. In arithmetic, for example, they'll do fine on small numbers and then fall apart on larger ones, even though the rules are exactly the same. That suggests they haven't really learned the general concept of arithmetic. They've learned a big collection of special cases. We saw something similar with the Go programs: they were superhuman, and yet it turned out they didn't correctly understand what a group of stones is. Fairly simple adversarial strategies could beat them.

So my view is that scaling is driving improvements partly because circuits are a fairly weak representation for many kinds of general knowledge. To approximate a concept that could be written down in a few lines of a more expressive language, you need an enormous circuit and enormous amounts of data. The scaling is in some sense compensating for the lack of the right kind of representation.

The concern is that we don't understand what's going on inside, so we can't predict when the next jump in capability will occur or what it will be. And we're also running out of text. There just isn't that much more high-quality human-written text in the universe to train on. So I would be surprised if pure scaling of this kind took us all the way to general-purpose AI. I think further conceptual breakthroughs will be needed. But I wouldn't bet the future of humanity on that being the case, and that's exactly why we need to take safety seriously now.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that we don't really know, and that's part of what worries me. What we can observe is that as you increase the amount of data and the amount of compute, performance on a wide range of benchmarks improves in a fairly predictable way. But the thing we're measuring is a kind of surface competence, and the question is what's happening underneath.

My best guess is that human text is produced by a process that involves reasoning, planning, factual knowledge about the world, and so on, and if you want to predict that text very accurately, you're forced to internalize at least some approximation of those underlying processes. So in some sense the model is being pushed toward building internal structures that function a little bit like world models, a little bit like logical inference, because that's what it takes to get the next word right. The driving force, if you like, is the pressure of the prediction task combined with enough capacity to actually represent those regularities.

But I'd put a very big asterisk on that. We're learning these systems by what amounts to a gigantic stochastic process. We don't understand the circuits that result. And it's entirely possible that what looks like reasoning is a very large collection of shallow heuristics that happen to cover the distribution we've tested. There's some evidence for that too, because you can find cases where the models fail on problems that are trivially easy once you change the surface form slightly. A system that really understood the underlying principle wouldn't be fooled that way.

So I'd say scaling works because the data contains the fingerprints of intelligence, and a sufficiently large network can pick up many of those fingerprints. Whether it's acquiring the real thing, or an increasingly convincing imitation of it, is a question I don't think the field has answered. And I'd add that even if scaling continues to deliver, it's an extraordinarily inefficient path. Humans learn from a tiny fraction of the data these systems consume, which suggests we're missing some fundamental ideas about how to build intelligent systems rather than just discovering that bigger is better.

astra-6.text:
I think the surprising thing is how much structure there is in language, and how much of the world’s structure is reflected in it. Predicting the next word sounds like a fairly superficial task. But if you’re going to do it really well, you have to capture something about what the speaker knows, what they’re trying to communicate, and how the world works.

As you increase the amount of data and the capacity of the model, it can pick up more of those relationships. And the training signal is available everywhere: every piece of text supplies examples, without someone having to label each one by hand.

But I would distinguish that explanation from a claim that we understand exactly what’s happening inside these systems. We don’t. We have very striking empirical results showing that scaling improves performance, but a much less complete account of what representations are being learned, why particular capabilities emerge, and where that process will run into limits.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main driving force is that predicting language well turns out to require much more than knowing about language. If you’re trying to predict what someone will say next, it helps to understand the world they’re talking about, what they know, and what they’re trying to achieve. So as you increase the amount of data and computation, there’s pressure to capture more of that underlying structure.

But we don’t yet have a very satisfactory explanation of why scaling works as well as it does, or how far it will take us. Better prediction produces some remarkably useful capabilities, but it doesn’t automatically give you reliable reasoning or a system that understands when its answer is wrong.
